newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish premier thanks Pope for political calm.
newsitem.headline: Polish premier thanks Pope for political calm.

text.p: Poland's ex-communist Prime Minister Wlodzimierz Cimoszewicz thanked Pope John Paul on Sunday for not stirring political debates during his trip to his homeland, which falls just four months before elections.

Cimoszewicz said he had also told the Pontiff, a stern critic of Western-style liberal values adopted by many Poles since the fall of communism eight years ago, not to worry about Poland because it was enjoying social and economic development.

"I expressed my...gratitude to the Pope for the fact that there is an atmosphere of calm, which we need so much, during his pilgrimage," Cimoszewicz said after a 20-minute meeting with the Pontiff in the Archbishop's residence in the southern city of Krakow.
"I also expressed the view that in thinking about his homeland, the Pope should be full of optimism because we will cope with the problems we have," he told a news conference.

The Pope, who ends his 11-day visit to Poland on Tuesday, has so far avoided direct remarks about politics even though he is known to sympathise with pro-Christian, right-leaning groups gathered around the Solidarity trade union.

Solidarity and its allies, for whom the Pope was a source of inspiration in the fight against communist rule before 1989, hope his current visit will boost them ahead of parliamentary polls due in September, when they aim to win power from Cimoszewicz's ex-communists.
The two groups are running neck-in-neck in opinion polls with about 25 percent of support each.
Cimoszewicz, whose Democratic Left Alliance (SLD) has been in power since 1993 together with a peasant party, said he had noted attempts to gain political capital from the visit.
"But I do not want to comment on them, so as not to spoil the special atmosphere accompanying this pilgrimage," he said.
The Solidarity alliance has put up huge posters across the country, depicting the Pope greeting crowds and bearing the group's logo next to the words "We are here, we remember."
Its leader Marian Krzaklewski, who has attended many of the masses celebrated by the pope, says the visit should prompt a "moral awakaning," which could help defeat the ex-communists.
Cimoszewicz said he and the Pope had not dicussed two issues that divide the Polish Church and the ex-communists most -- abortion and a so-far unratified concordat treaty with the Vatican.
